idea: The Beaufort scale as a vertical chart: thirteen tiny line-drawn sea states from a flat mirror to a white storm, with the original wording at the ends, 'Force 0: Sea like a mirror' down to 'Force 12: The air is filled with foam and spray.' A sailor's ladder of calm to fury, drawn in code.

The Plimsoll load line: the ring with the horizontal bar and the lettered marks TF, F, T, S, W, WNA, drawn like a ship-hull side elevation, caption 'Know when to stop.' Made law in Britain in 1876 after too many overloaded ships went down; a shirt about limits.

A chart of the longitude problem: a globe cut into 24 time slices of 15 degrees each, caption 'One hour = 15 degrees. Knowing the hour at home was the whole problem.' For anyone who loves that a clock solved navigation (Harrison).

Spring and neap tides: Sun, Moon and Earth drawn in line and at right angles, with the two resulting tide curves beneath, caption 'Two bodies, one pull.' Footnote line: 'Bay of Fundy: a tidal range of up to 16 metres.'

A square-rigger in side elevation with every sail labelled in tiny type, from flying jib to spanker and royal to course, caption 'Every sail has a name.' A nautical-nerd diagram that looks like an old plate.

A deep-dive depth chart: a vertical scale in metres with the Cuvier's beaked whale's record dive marked at 2,992 m (recorded 2014), with the sperm whale and elephant seal above it and the Titanic wreck's depth line for comparison. Caption: 'Mammals. Holding their breath.'

The 32-point compass rose with every point named in full ('North by east', 'North-northeast', 'Northeast by north'...) around the rim, caption 'Boxing the compass.' Type and line only; reciting the points was how sailors learned to steer.

The chip log: a drawing of the wooden quadrant, the line with knots tied every 47 feet 3 inches, and the 28-second sandglass, caption 'Why a knot is a knot.' Explains the unit of ship speed by the thing sailors actually threw overboard.

Ocean zones as a cross-section from surface to abyss with sunlight fading to nothing by about 1,000 m, small animal silhouettes in each band, caption 'Below here, the only light is made by the animals.' Many deep-sea animals produce their own light.

A Fresnel lighthouse lens in cross-section: concentric glass prisms bending one lamp into a single beam, caption 'One flame, bent into a beam.' Augustin Fresnel's design replaced mirrors in the 1820s and is why lighthouses could shrink and shine farther.

The Draupner wave record: the actual wave-height trace as a line drawn from the data's shape, with the spike labelled '25.6 m, 1 January 1995, North Sea' and the caption 'Until then, rogue waves were a sailor's story.' The first measured proof of one.

The anatomy of a wave: the circles water particles trace beneath a wave, shrinking with depth until they vanish, caption 'The wave travels. The water mostly stays.' A diagram that quietly corrects what everyone pictures.

A cross-section of the warship Vasa with gun decks and ballast marked, caption 'Vasa, 1628. Sailed about 1,300 metres.' She capsized on her maiden voyage in Stockholm harbour and was raised in 1961; dark humour for the over-ambitious.
A to-scale vertical comparison: Mount Everest (8,849 m) drawn upside down into the Challenger Deep (about 10,935 m), caption 'Drop Everest in. There's still two kilometres of water on top.'

River meander cut-off in four plan views: bend tightens, neck narrows, river breaks through, oxbow lake left behind, caption 'The Mississippi shortened itself 242 miles in 176 years.' (Mark Twain's figure in Life on the Mississippi.)

Luke Howard's clouds: cirrus, cumulus, stratus and nimbus drawn as a simple altitude cross-section with their Latin names, caption 'Named in 1802 by a pharmacist.' Howard's classification is still the basis of cloud naming.
A hurricane in cross-section: eyewall, rainbands, inflow arrows at the bottom and outflow at the top, with a clear calm eye in the middle, caption 'The calm is in the middle.'

Two ships to scale on one baseline: Columbus's Santa Maria (about 20 m) beside a modern container ship (about 400 m, like the Ever Ace), caption 'Same ocean.' Silhouettes only; the size gap says everything.

A ship's stability diagram: a hull heeled over, the centre of gravity, centre of buoyancy and metacentre marked with arrows for the righting lever, caption 'Why ships come back up.' A pleasing statement about resilience, true physics.

A Mercator map with Greenland and Africa side by side, Africa then shown at its real size (about 30 million km2 against Greenland's 2.2 million), caption 'Mercator, 1569: wrong about size, right about bearing.' A fair defence of a famous distortion: a straight line there is a constant compass course.
